site: Great Zimbabwe (great_zimbabwe, chapter 9, Africa and the Indian Ocean): the Great Enclosure and its conical tower, near Masvingo, Zimbabwe, about 20.27 S 30.93 E (the atlas coordinates match the site). The Great Enclosure's outer wall is generally dated to the 14th century (one summary gives the tower as 13th to 14th century), within the site's 11th to 15th century occupation. It was built by the ancestors of Shona-speaking people.
view: Stand inside the Great Enclosure, in the court around the conical tower: the space between the older inner ('old') wall and the outer wall, which the Parallel Passage and a doorway through the old wall lead into. Stand a few to perhaps 15 m from the tower on its north-west side (the court's real depth is not verified; check a measured plan), at standing eye height, looking roughly south-east toward the tower and the south-east stretch of the outer wall behind it. In frame: the conical tower at full height, left of centre, standing on bare ground. The smaller, damaged second tower stands beside it; check which side on a measured plan (see contested). Behind both, the inside face of the outer wall curves across the whole width of the plate. Near the tower the wall and the tower are about the same height: one field guide says the tower is a little higher than the wall at this point, and other accounts give the wall a maximum of about 11 m, above the tower's 9 to 10 m. So the wall's top edge lands near the tower's top in the picture, just below it or just above it; never far below it. A strip of brochure sky sits over the wall, with the crowns of one or two woodland trees beyond it. Cropped: the wall runs out of both sides of the frame. The Hill Complex lies north, behind and to the left of the viewer, and the wall would hide it anyway, so it is out of frame. The chevron band is on the outer face of the wall and cannot be seen from this spot. Optional, and only if the measured plan confirms it can be seen from here: the old wall with the doorway into the tower court (dark amphibolite courses on each side) and the stepped platform beside it, or the rounded end of a wall with the narrow dark slot of the Parallel Passage. If the standpoint puts the old wall between the viewer and the tower's foot, that stretch of old wall is left out (see deliberatelyWrong). Why this view: it is the view most photographs of the tower take, tower against wall. From outside close to the wall the tower is hidden or shows at most as a sliver of its top, because the two are about the same height and stand close together. It is also the view the ruling allows (walls, passage and tower). And at 92 x 70 it reads as a silhouette: a tapering, flat-topped cone against a long, level band.

elements.fact: A solid, tapering tower of dry granite, about 9 m (30 ft) to nearly 10 m tall and about 5.5 m (18 ft) across at the base; it narrows markedly toward the top, where it may be about 2 m across (the top width is not verified; see contested). A truncated cone with a flat, slightly ragged top: not pointed, not domed. The sides slope in and swell slightly outward (a field guide describes it as 'plain' with 'sloping sides swelling slightly'), so the profile is a gently convex taper, not a ruled straight cone and not a beehive. The top once carried a dentelle course that is now gone. No door, window, stair, ledge or internal chamber. Bent dug around it in 1891, destroying the stratigraphy. It stands inside the enclosure, between the old inner wall and the outer wall, close to the south-east stretch of the outer wall. Its courses are regular and horizontal (Whitty's Q style).

It exists and stands beside the great tower: the 'small conical tower'. Its summit was pushed over by a large tree trunk; photographs of 1891 show it then almost intact. It is clearly smaller than the great tower; its exact height, diameter and which side it stands on are not verified (see contested).

elements.element: Outer wall of the Great Enclosure, seen from the inside
elements.fact: Dry-stone granite with no mortar. The largest single ancient structure south of the Sahara. It runs about 250 m (252 m in one summary) around. Its maximum height is given as about 11 m in most summaries, but one field guide gives 9.6 m at most and about 7 m on average; near the tower it is about the tower's height (see contested). About 5 m thick at the base and tapering toward the top, so the faces batter, leaning back as they rise. The wall curves in plan and has no corners. Its top reads as a level line. Its highest and best-built stretch is the south-east one, near the tower: rectangular blocks laid in relatively even and level courses (Whitty's 'Q' style).

Local granite, split from the exfoliating granite domes into roughly rectangular, brick-to-block-sized pieces. They are laid in thin, continuous, level courses with dry joints: no mortar and no plaster. The joints read as fine dark lines. Exception: the doorway into the tower court through the old wall is decorated on each side with courses of dark amphibolite.

elements.element: Inner wall end and Parallel Passage (optional)
elements.fact: A long, narrow and tightening corridor runs between the outer wall and an older, rougher inner wall ('P' style). It leads from the north-east entrance of the enclosure (some plans call it the north entrance) to the area around the conical tower. A doorway leading to the tower was inserted in the old wall, with courses of dark amphibolite on each side, and beside it a platform about 7.6 m (25 ft) across, the largest at Great Zimbabwe, rises in steps to the top of the old wall. Where a wall ends at an opening, the end is rounded, never square. Paint any of this only if the measured plan shows it can be seen from the chosen standpoint.

Not in frame. A band of double chevron (zigzag) coursing, split by a horizontal line, about 50 cm high, runs near the top of the outer face of the outer wall, about 9 m above the ground, along only the south-eastern arc: 'nearly 80 metres' of the roughly 250 m circuit by one account (older figures around 52 m also circulate; see contested). From inside the enclosure it cannot be seen. The chevron is not the same pattern as dentelle, which is a single course of stones set on edge at an angle, like saw teeth.
Open, level ground of grey-tan granite sand with short grass. Bent dug around the tower in 1891, and Hall cleared deposits from the interior in 1902 to 1904. No paving.
The site lies in miombo savanna woodland on the plateau at roughly 1,100 m, with broad-leaved trees such as msasa. No palms, no rainforest, no desert. (Not re-checked on the web in this run.)
The set's shared brochure sky. Take a dry-season clear day, which is the tourist season.
The granite hill with walls and boulders, north of the Great Enclosure. It is the revered locus and stays out of frame (gate 6).

mustBeRight: One large tower: a truncated cone with a flat top. It is not pointed and not domed.
The large tower is about 1.6 to 1.8 times as tall as it is wide at the base.
The tower tapers from base to top. Its sides are straight or very slightly convex (they swell a little); never concave, never a bulging beehive.
The tower has no door, window, stair, ledge or opening anywhere.
A second, smaller tower stands beside the large one, lower and damaged at the top.
The towers stand inside the enclosure, in front of the inside face of the outer wall.

The outer wall's top edge in the picture is close to the large tower's top, just below or just above it, and in any case well above the tower's mid-height. The wall is never drawn as a low parapet with the tower rising far above it.
The outer wall curves across the frame, with a level top line.
The wall faces lean back as they rise (the wall is about 5 m thick at the base and tapers). They are not vertical.
All stonework is shown as thin level courses of small rectangular blocks.
No mortar lines, no plaster, no large ashlar blocks.
There is no chevron or zigzag pattern on the tower or on the inside face of the wall.
No hill, rocky outcrop or boulders appear on the skyline.
No bird carvings and no stone pillars with carvings on them.
No people, no offerings, no ritual objects.
The trees beyond the wall are broad-leaved savanna trees. No palms.
deliberatelyWrong: No visitors, guides, walkways, signs, ropes or site museum. The brochure clears the site of everything modern.

The interior is shown as clean ground and short grass. The inner walls, platforms, remains of clay house floors, and plants growing on the walls are left out so that the tower and wall read at 92 x 70. If the chosen standpoint puts the old inner wall or the stepped platform between the viewer and the tower's foot, that stretch is left out too.
Courses are suggested, not counted. The real coursing is too fine to show course by course at this size, so the bands are fewer and bolder than the real ones.
The stone is cleaned up. Lichen, rust staining and rain streaks are reduced to a few accents, as a brochure's printing would.

The light is the set's fixed upper-right sun, not the sun's true position for this standpoint and date. It was not computed. As a sanity check only: facing roughly south-east in the late dry season (September to October), an afternoon sun in the west sits behind and to the right of the viewer, so an upper-right light is loosely plausible; in the mid dry season (June to July) the sun stands in the north, behind-left, and it would not be.
The wall's curve is simplified to one clean sweep, and later repairs and reconstructed stretches are not told apart from original fabric.
The tower's top is painted plain and slightly ragged, as it stands now. The dentelle course that once ran round its top is gone and is not restored.

lighting: Bright, clear dry-season sun from the upper right (B.LIGHT). The round tower gets a lit right flank and a shaded left flank with a soft terminator, and the upper edge of each course picks up a thin highlight over a dark joint. The tower's top is lit. The inside face of the curving wall darkens from lit to shaded as it turns away from the light. The tower may cast a shadow to the left onto the ground and onto the wall behind it (B.castShadow). Shadows are the set's cool violet (B.C.shadow mixed in), never black. Sanity check, not a computed position: at about 20 S, a late-dry-season (September to October) afternoon sun in the west lies behind-right of a viewer facing south-east, which loosely matches; the set's convention decides the light.
pitfalls: Painting the tower as a pointed cone, a spire or a beehive dome. It is a flat-topped truncated cone whose sides swell only slightly.

Showing the tower from outside, rising over a low wall. The outer wall near it is about as tall as the tower (a little lower by one account, taller by others) and stands close to it, so from outside the tower is hidden or shows at most as a sliver.
Mortar lines, big squared blocks, or plastered walls. This is dry stone: small blocks in thin courses.
Adding a door, a window, a stair or a doorway at the base of the tower. It is solid.
Square corners or vertical wall faces. The walls curve in plan, have rounded ends at openings and lean back as they rise.
Putting the chevron on the tower, on the inside face of the wall, or all the way round the wall. It runs only along the top of the outer face of the south-eastern arc.
Treating chevron and dentelle as the same pattern (the task brief calls them 'chevron (dentelle)'). Chevron is a zigzag band. Dentelle is a single course of stones set at an angle, like saw teeth.
Drawing the small tower as a near-twin of the large one. It is smaller and its summit is damaged.

Painting the whole scene in one granite colour when the old wall's doorway is in frame: that doorway is edged on each side with courses of dark amphibolite. Conversely, do not put dark bands anywhere else.
Cold blue-grey granite, or a yellow sandstone warmth borrowed from Egypt. It is warm pale grey with dark streaks.
Putting the Hill Complex or its boulders on the horizon because they are famous. The ruling keeps them out of frame.
A soapstone Zimbabwe Bird on a pillar as a flourish. It is excluded, and none came from the Great Enclosure in any case.

Anything Near Eastern, Phoenician or Sabaean in the styling, or 'King Solomon's Mines' romance: no temple framing, no altar, no exotic figures, no palms, no jungle. A real mid-century Rhodesian brochure would have printed that myth. This one must not.
Using the nineteenth-century plates' captions or text. Only the drawings and photographs are reference, as the site looked in 1891 to 1905. Bent's and Hall's text attributes the builders wrongly.
gate6: The arc does not name the revered locus. The literature points to the Hill Complex: the granite hill north of the Great Enclosure, formerly called the 'Acropolis', with its caves and its Eastern Enclosure. Local communities regard Great Zimbabwe as sacred and tied to their ancestors, with rituals connected to water and fertility (Ndoro, ICCROM Conservation Studies 4, 2005, 'Your Monument Our Shrine', confirmed as a publication in this run; its content was seen only in a search summary). Oral tradition connects the Hill's cave to the voice of the ancestors and to rain-making, and the Eastern Enclosure is where the soapstone birds stood. The literature names local clans (Nemanwa, Mugabe, Charumbira among them) with ceremonies at the site; these names were not confirmed in this run and must not be relied on without re-reading Ndoro. The vignette must not show: (1) the Hill Complex in any form, including the hill, its walls, its balanced boulders, its caves and the Eastern Enclosure; (2) any soapstone Zimbabwe Bird or carved stone pillar (sacred objects, repatriated, and the national emblem); (3) any ceremony, offering, beer or snuff pot, spirit medium, or praying or kneeling figure; (4) any grave, burial or human remains; (5) any people at all. The Great Enclosure's outer wall, the Parallel Passage and the two towers are inside the ruling. Also do not use Bent's name 'the Temple' for the Great Enclosure, or anything that turns the enclosure into a shrine (an altar, offerings at the tower's foot).
contested: Tower dimensions: commonly cited as about 9 m (30 ft) tall, by others 'nearly 10 metres', and about 5.5 m (18 ft) across the base (both confirmed in search summaries this run). The top width of about 2 m was not confirmed. Some of the height difference may be the lost dentelle course and top courses. Keep the proportions and do not paint to an exact metre.

Outer wall height, and the tower-to-wall height relation near the tower: most summaries give a maximum of about 11 m (Wikipedia and Smarthistory, via search summaries). The Zimbabwe Field Guide gives 9.6 m at most and about 7 m on average, and says the conical tower 'is a little higher than the Outer Wall at this point'. So near the tower the two are about the same height, and which is higher is unsettled. Thickness about 5 m at the base (field guide); circuit about 250 m (252 m in one summary).

What the conical tower was for: a symbolic granary standing for a ruler's tribute and generosity (the reading Garlake reports, following Shona tradition); a male or phallic symbol tied to initiation (Huffman 1996); a lookout. None is proven. Paint nothing that implies a use.
What the Great Enclosure was for: a royal residence or the royal wives' quarters (Garlake 1973), or an initiation school (domba, Huffman 1996). The colonial-era 'Temple' reading is rejected.

What the chevron means: Huffman ties it to male authority and rain, and others differ. Its position, near the top of the outer face of the south-eastern arc, about 9 m above the ground, is not in dispute. Its length is: the Zimbabwe Field Guide says 'nearly 80 metres' of double chevron; the figure of about 52 m in the earlier draft of this spec was not confirmed.

Chronology: Huffman and Vogel (1991) give a sequence of Hill, then Great Enclosure, then Valley. Chirikure et al. (2013, Bayesian model) argue that construction overlapped. The Great Enclosure's outer wall is usually put in the 14th century.
The name: 'dzimba dza mabwe' (houses of stone) or 'dzimba woye' (venerated houses, used of chiefs' houses or graves). Both derivations are current.

Unverified, not disputed. The second tower's height and diameter, and which side of the great tower it stands on. Confirmed only that it exists, is smaller, and that its summit was pushed over by a tree after 1891. The current code draws it at about half the great tower's height, which may be too large. Check a measured plan (Caton-Thompson 1931, Garlake 1973, the NMMZ plan) before painting.

The tower's top: the Zimbabwe Field Guide says it 'once had a dentelle pattern which is now gone'; a low-reliability study page speaks of a dentelle frieze round the top as if present. Paint the top plain and slightly ragged, as it stands now; do not restore the dentelle.

Unverified, not disputed. Early accounts report monoliths and small turrets on the top of the outer wall above the chevron stretch. Whether any stand where they could be seen from inside is unchecked. Leave the wall top plain unless the check confirms them.

The tower court: the tower stands between the old inner wall and the outer wall, reached by the Parallel Passage and by a doorway inserted in the old wall, with a stepped platform about 7.6 m across beside it. How deep the court is, and so how far back the viewer can stand, was not verified. Check a measured plan before fixing the standpoint.
Parallel Passage entrance: one summary says it runs from the north-eastern entrance; the earlier draft said the north entrance. Check the plan; it matters only if the passage mouth is painted.

sources.title: Gertrude Caton-Thompson, The Zimbabwe Culture: Ruins and Reactions (Oxford: Clarendon, 1931)
sources.detail: British Association excavation of 1929. Settled that the builders were African, with measured plans and sections of the Great Enclosure and tower. Not public domain (US public domain only from 1 January 2027; UK and EU 2056). Use for measurements on screen only.

sources.title: David Randall-MacIver, Mediaeval Rhodesia (London: Macmillan, 1906)
sources.detail: First professional excavation (1905). Argued for African builders and a medieval date against Bent and Hall. Photographs and plans are public domain. The preferred public-domain visual reference, and its text is right.

sources.title: J. Theodore Bent, The Ruined Cities of Mashonaland (London: Longmans, 1892), with plans by R. M. W. Swan
sources.detail: Public-domain plates of the tower and walls as they stood in 1891, before Hall's clearance. The text is the documented Phoenician/Arab misattribution: use the drawings only, never the text.

sources.title: R. N. Hall, Great Zimbabwe, Mashonaland, Rhodesia (London: Methuen, 1905); Hall and Neal, The Ancient Ruins of Rhodesia (1902)
sources.detail: Public-domain photographs of the conical tower and enclosure. Hall's 1902 to 1904 clearance destroyed deposits inside the Great Enclosure. His text is the foreign-builder error; use only as a picture of the ruin c. 1902.

sources.title: Carl Mauch, journals and plans of 1871, published in Petermanns Geographische Mitteilungen, Ergänzungsheft 37 (1874)
sources.detail: Earliest European plan and sketches of the ruins. Public domain. His Queen of Sheba attribution is the first of the foreign-builder claims and is excluded.

sources.title: Anthony Whitty, 'The origins of the stone architecture of Zimbabwe', Proceedings of the First Federal Science Congress (Salisbury, 1961)
sources.detail: The P, Q and R wall styles: Q is the regular coursing of the Great Enclosure's outer wall and the tower; P is the older, rougher inner wall.

sources.title: Thomas N. Huffman, Snakes and Crocodiles: Power and Symbolism in Ancient Zimbabwe (Johannesburg: Witwatersrand University Press, 1996)
sources.detail: Symbolic readings of the Great Enclosure (initiation), the tower and the chevron. Cited for the disputes, not as settled fact.

sources.title: Webber Ndoro, Your Monument Our Shrine: The Preservation of Great Zimbabwe (Uppsala, Studies in African Archaeology 19, 2001); and ICCROM Conservation Studies 4 (2005)
sources.detail: Local communities' spiritual relationship to the site, the sacred standing of the Hill Complex, and conservation of the walls (lichen, plant growth, reconstruction). Basis for the gate-6 answer. The 2005 ICCROM edition was confirmed as a publication in this run (ICCROM publication page, https://www.iccrom.org/publication/preservation-great-zimbabwe-your-monument-our-shrine), and a search summary confirmed local beliefs of sacredness, ancestral connection and rituals of water and fertility. The text itself was not re-read; the clan names are unconfirmed.

repoCorrections: content/map/README.md, vignettes table, chapter 9 row, 'The conical tower seen over the enclosure wall': from outside this is at best a sliver. The outer wall beside the tower is about the tower's height (9.6 to 11 m against 9 to 10 m, depending on the source) and stands close to it. The row should say the tower is seen from inside the Great Enclosure, standing in front of the inside face of the outer wall. The rest of the row is right: the smaller second tower whose summit has fallen; dry stone, no mortar, no door, no stair, solid.
src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower' doc comment, 'seen over the outer wall': the same error.

src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower', proportions: the wall is drawn in front of the towers with its top at y of about 51 to 56 over a ground at y 72, while the great tower rises to y of about 12. That makes the tower about three times the height of a wall that is actually about as tall as it. The wall should be behind the towers, with its top near the tower's top.
src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower', summit: the great tower's top is drawn as a dome raised 4 units above the shoulders (quadraticCurveTo). The real tower is flat-topped (truncated).

src/map/monuments.ts, 'conical-tower', small tower: drawn at about half the great tower's height and 60% of its base width. On the standard photographs it looks much smaller than that. Check a measured plan and resize.

content/research/arc.md section 7, 'any pre-Bent attribution of Great Zimbabwe to Phoenicians or Sheba': read literally, this excludes only claims made before Bent. The exclusion should cover every foreign-builder attribution: Mauch 1871 (Sheba), Bent 1892 (Phoenician/Arab), Hall 1902 to 1905 (Phoenician/Sabaean), and the Rhodesian-era guidebooks that repeated them. Randall-MacIver (1906) and Caton-Thompson (1931) are the correction.

content/research/arc.md chapter 9 table, Great Zimbabwe row, 'Hill Complex on kopje, 11 m drystone wall, conical tower': the 11 m wall belongs to the Great Enclosure, not the Hill Complex. The row also leads with the Hill Complex, the part the 2026-09-23 ruling puts out of frame. The row, or the ruling, should name the revered locus as the Hill Complex, with its caves, the Eastern Enclosure and the birds, so that no later designer has to guess.

content/research/arc.md chapter 9 imagery line and section 6: for Great Zimbabwe specifically there is public-domain imagery beyond 'Bent 1892': Mauch 1871 to 1874, Hall 1902 and 1905, and Randall-MacIver 1906. Randall-MacIver is the one whose text is also right. The 'weakest in the game' rating fits the coastal sites, not this one.
confidence: Medium overall; medium-high for the shape and material facts, medium-low for exact figures and the standpoint. In this run 12 of 12 allowed web searches were used and are now exhausted; WebFetch was refused by the egress proxy for every host tried (zimfieldguide.com, smarthistory.org, metmuseum.org, ronperrier.net, web.mit.edu, worldhistory.org, readingroo.ms), so every check rests on search-result summaries, not on read pages. Confirmed that way: dry-stone granite with no mortar; rectangular blocks in level courses; outer wall about 250 m round and about 5 m thick at the base, tapering; chevron near the top of the outer face of the south-eastern arc; tower about 9 m to nearly 10 m by 5.5 m, solid, no door, chamber or stair; the small tower exists and its summit fell; the Parallel Passage leads to the tower; the doorway and stepped platform in the old wall; Ndoro's publication and local sacred regard. Corrected: the wall near the tower is about the tower's height, not clearly taller (one source says the tower is a little higher); the tower's sides swell slightly rather than tapering as a ruled cone; the chevron runs 'nearly 80 metres', not 52 m; the tower's top had a dentelle course, now gone; the passage starts at the north-east entrance by one summary. Still unverified: the tower's top width; the small tower's size and side; the depth of the tower court and so the standpoint distance; rounded wall ends; the flat, level wall top; the granite colour and palette; the clan names in gate6; the vegetation and altitude. Check these against Garlake 1973, Caton-Thompson 1931 and the NMMZ plan before the asset note is committed.
